theme: Levitical genealogies; Jerusalem after the exile [survey]
readingInstruction: Read 1 Chronicles 6:1-9:44. This is the last survey reading from the genealogies. Pay attention to the Levites, who serve in worship, and to the people who returned to Jerusalem at the end of chapter 9.
settingTheScene: The Chronicler gives special attention to the tribe of Levi, because the temple and its worship were central for the returned community. Chapter 6 lists the priestly line from Aaron and the singers appointed by David. Chapter 9 ends the genealogies with a roll call of those who returned from exile and lived in Jerusalem. The introduction is over, and the story of David begins in chapter 10.
observation: “These are the men whom David put in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD” (6:31).
“And they ministered with song before the tabernacle of the tent of meeting” (6:32).
“But Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering” (6:49).
“All these, chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212” (9:22).
“Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants” (9:2).
“And some of the sons of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem” (9:3).
“Some of them had charge of the vessels of service” (9:28).
“They were in the singers, the heads of fathers” houses of the Levites, dwelling in the chambers of the temple, free from other service, for they were on duty day and night’ (9:33).
interpretation:
The Levites are given a large place for a reason. The Chronicler wanted the community to remember that worship is not an afterthought. After the exile, with no king, the temple and its worship were the center of national life. Levi’s line is listed in detail: the gatekeepers, the singers, and the priests. Even the musicians are named. David appointed men to the service of song, and they “ministered with song” before the tabernacle until Solomon built the temple.

This is one of the Chronicler’s emphases. Music is ministry. Those who sang were serving in the house of the LORD, just as those who offered sacrifices. The worship of God deserves skill, order, and care. Chapter 9 says some singers were “on duty day and night.” There was constant praise.

Chapter 9 ends with the list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. It mirrors the lists in Nehemiah 11. After the long genealogy, we arrive at the present: the people are back, the city is occupied, the work of worship resumes. The genealogy is not an empty record. It leads to the community that is reading it.

Then the chapter ends with a reminder of King Saul’s genealogy, and immediately chapter 10 will tell of his death. The mood shifts. The introduction is over. The Chronicler has given us a map of the people. Now he will tell the story.

Do not be discouraged if these chapters feel dry. They are the foundation. Everything that follows, the story of David’s kingdom and the temple, rests on the belief that God knows his people by name and has a place for each.
connection: 1 Peter 2:9 calls the church a royal priesthood. Hebrews 4:14-16 names Jesus as our great high priest. Revelation 1:6 says he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father. Ephesians 5:19 says to sing and make melody to the Lord with your heart. Colossians 3:16 mentions teaching one another with psalms and hymns. Romans 12:1 invites us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice.
application:
Think about those who serve behind the scenes in your church, such as musicians, ushers, and volunteers. Thank one of them.

If you have a musical or creative gift, ask how God might use it in worship.

Practice offering your ordinary work as service to God.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he has a place for each person in his work.
Thank someone who serves behind the scenes.
Ask him to show you your place.
